## Working Papers

::: {.paper}
::: {.paper-title}
Wages, amenities and the value of formal employment: A structural approach for Mexico
:::

<details class="abstract">
<summary>Abstract</summary>
<div class="abstract-body">
Workers move frequently between formal and informal jobs, yet the motives behind
these transitions remain debated. Using household survey data from Mexico, I
document that most informal-to-formal transitions take place within the same
firm, consistent with a foot-in-the-door route to formality, and that sustained
formalisation raises hourly wages only modestly. The wage gain is concentrated
among low-skilled workers, even though skilled workers formalise at higher rates.
These limited wage gains suggest that workers accept formal employment for
reasons beyond current wage. I estimate a two-sector search model in which
informal workers receive formal offers both from outside firms and from their
current employer, and decompose the value of formal employment into a
sector-specific non-wage amenity, future job opportunities, and employment
stability. The estimated formal-sector amenity is worth 29.4% of the median
informal wage for skilled men and 15.2% for skilled women, is negative for
low-skilled women, and is not statistically significant for low-skilled men.
Future formal job opportunities also contribute substantially to acceptance of
formality; the within-firm foot-in-the-door channel is worth about 16% of the
median informal wage for skilled men and about 4% for low-skilled women, and is
quantitatively important for employment. In the absence of this channel, formal
employment drops by roughly 8–14 percentage points for men and about 1–2 points
for women, while informality and non-employment increase.
</div>
</details>
:::
